title: Administration Spends 4 Billion Buying Back Offshore Wind Leases
description_short: Administration Spends 4 Billion Buying Back Offshore Wind Leases
description_medium: The Trump administration reached a 1.2 billion settlement to buy back offshore wind leases, bringing total buyback spending to nearly 4 billion across multiple deals. Trump stated his goal is to prevent any windmills from being built. Sen. Whitehouse called the buybacks an effective bribe to push companies away from clean energy.
description_long: The Trump administration reached a reported $1.2 billion settlement to buy back offshore wind leases, bringing spending across multiple lease buybacks to nearly $4 billion, according to the linked AP report. President Trump said his goal was to prevent wind turbines from being built. The entry records a policy choice to pay companies to relinquish projects rather than allow the leases to proceed; it does not establish that every proposed wind project would otherwise have been completed or that the full reported total came from one agreement. Senator Whitehouse criticized the buybacks as an effective bribe to push companies away from clean energy. That is his characterization of the policy, not a court finding. The scale of the spending and the administration's stated objective raise questions about the use of public resources and the government's energy priorities. The AP account is needed to assess the separate deals, recipients, funding source, and any conditions attached to the settlement. Those details would clarify how the nearly $4 billion total was calculated and what obligations the companies accepted.

title: USAID Dismantled Using Russian Disinformation as Pretext
description_short: USAID Dismantled Using Russian Disinformation as Pretext
description_medium: In February 2025, false claims about USAID spending circulated as the Trump administration moved to dismantle the agency. The supplied account says Karoline Leavitt repeated unsupported spending figures, while Trump allies shared a fabricated video falsely linking USAID to celebrity trips in Ukraine. The linked New York Times report examines how these claims fueled the campaign against the foreign-aid agency.
description_long: In February 2025, the Trump administration moved to gut USAID — cutting its workforce from 10,000 to under 300 — while flooding social media with documented falsehoods to justify the action. Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt falsely claimed at a February 4 briefing that USAID spent '$47,000 for a transgender opera in Colombia' and '$32,000 for a transgender comic book in Peru.' Elon Musk and Donald Trump Jr. amplified a fabricated E! News video — traced to a Russian disinformation network called Pravda — falsely claiming USAID paid celebrities like Ben Stiller and Angelina Jolie for Ukraine propaganda trips. Trump separately claimed USAID sent '$50 million in condoms to Hamas,' a claim fact-checked as false by multiple outlets including DW and Reuters. The AP reported the disinformation campaign was a coordinated effort to manufacture public consent for dismantling a 60-year-old foreign aid institution.

title: Eric Adams Corruption Charges Dropped in Exchange for Immigration Cooperation
description_short: Eric Adams Corruption Charges Dropped in Exchange for Immigration Cooperation
description_medium: In February 2025, the Justice Department directed prosecutors to drop the corruption case against New York City Mayor Eric Adams, whose indictment involved alleged bribes from Turkish officials. Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove cited Adams's cooperation with the administration's immigration policy; prosecutors resigned in protest. A judge later dismissed the case with prejudice and criticized the department's rationale as resembling a bargain.
description_long: In February 2025, the Trump DOJ directed federal prosecutors in New York to drop corruption charges against Democratic NYC Mayor Eric Adams. Acting Deputy AG Emil Bove's memo stated the September 2024 indictment — charging Adams with accepting bribes from Turkish officials — was interfering with Adams' capacity to support Trump's immigration crackdown and his 2025 re-election campaign. Eight federal prosecutors resigned in protest, describing the move as an unlawful quid pro quo. U.S. Attorney for Manhattan Danielle Sassoon also resigned rather than comply, writing that Bove had designs on dropping charges before their conversation. In a 78-page ruling on April 2, 2025, U.S. District Judge Dale Ho dismissed the case with prejudice, writing that the DOJ's rationale smacks of a bargain: dismissal of the indictment in exchange for immigration policy concessions, and found the pressure disturbing. The dismissal with prejudice meant prosecutors could not refile after the mayoral election.

title: Operation Epic Fury: Trump's Iran War Begins Without Congressional Authorization, Ends in Chaos
description_short: Operation Epic Fury: Trump's Iran War Begins Without Congressional Authorization, Ends in Chaos
description_medium: The supplied long account describes the February 2026 U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran, later ceasefire and renewed conflict, and their claimed regional and economic effects. The only linked source is a congressional resolution concerning hostilities; it does not substantiate the full sequence, the agreement's terms, casualty figures, or polling result. Those reports are needed before this entry can be completed.
description_long: On February 28, 2026, U.S. and Israeli forces launched coordinated strikes on Iran — Operation Epic Fury — without a congressional declaration of war or AUMF, with Trump claiming the goal was to eliminate imminent threats from the Iranian regime. The 39-day bombing campaign killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and dozens of Iranian military leaders but failed to achieve regime change, force denuclearization, or stop Iran's missile program. After an initial ceasefire collapsed, Trump signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Iran on June 18, 2026, at Versailles — widely condemned as appeasement — pledging billions in sanctions relief and reconstruction assistance in exchange for Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz. When Iran resumed attacks on merchant shipping in July 2026, Trump declared the deal over and authorized new strikes, plunging the region back into conflict. The Strait of Hormuz remained partially closed — a chokepoint for 20% of the world's oil and gas — while 60% of Americans told Quinnipiac pollsters the Iran war was not worth it. Council on Foreign Relations analysts concluded Trump had launched a war of choice with no exit strategy, no congressional authorization, and no viable military path to his stated objectives.

title: Trump Says He’d Bring Back Waterboarding and “A Hell of a Lot Worse”
description_short: Trump Says He’d Bring Back Waterboarding and “A Hell of a Lot Worse”
description_medium: During the 2016 campaign, Trump said he would restore waterboarding and use methods “a hell of a lot worse.” The Hill report and PolitiFact promise entry document the remark and its place in his public position on interrogation. This entry records campaign rhetoric, not an order authorizing torture or evidence that the proposal was carried out.
description_long: During the 2016 presidential campaign, Donald Trump said the United States should bring back waterboarding and that he would support methods “a hell of a lot worse.” The linked Hill article reported the statement, while PolitiFact tracked the pledge as a promise to restore waterboarding. The remark was more than a general expression of toughness: it proposed reviving an interrogation method that had been prohibited by U.S. law and international commitments, and suggested going beyond it. The supplied reporting supports describing Trump's public position and the concern it raised about torture, but it does not show that he issued an order to use waterboarding or that any such practice resumed because of the statement. Keeping the event at the level of a campaign pledge distinguishes rhetoric from government action. The episode is relevant to human-rights protections because a candidate seeking executive authority was publicly advocating coercive interrogation. The linked sources do not identify a specific operational plan or measure what effect the comments had on policy or public opinion.

title: Floats Buying Greenland
description_short: Reports said Trump had discussed the idea of the United States buying Greenland, an idea dismissed by Danish officials and widely criticized as a colonial-style fantasy.
description_medium: In 2019, reports said Donald Trump had discussed whether the United States could buy Greenland. Danish officials rejected the idea, and Greenland's government said the island was not for sale. The linked report describes a reported proposal and public response, not a formal offer, negotiations, or an agreement to transfer the territory.
description_long: In August 2019, news reports said Donald Trump had discussed the idea of the United States buying Greenland. Danish officials rejected the proposal, and Greenland's government said the island was not for sale. Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark, so the idea concerned the sovereignty and political choices of its residents as well as U.S.-Danish relations. The supplied account documents discussion of a possible purchase and the public rejection; it does not establish that the United States made a formal offer, opened negotiations, or secured Greenlandic consent. No transaction took place in the account. That distinction matters because a reported idea should not be described as a completed diplomatic initiative or an agreed sale. The episode drew attention to how a president's comments about another territory can affect relations with an ally and prompt a response from the people whose status is at issue. The linked CNBC story's headline reports the refusal; its page was unavailable during the focused read, so further details about the discussion and the Danish response remain unverified.

title: Trump Campaign Uses AI Deepfakes of Taylor Swift Endorsing Him
description_short: Trump Campaign Uses AI Deepfakes of Taylor Swift Endorsing Him
description_medium: In August 2024, Trump shared AI-generated images that falsely portrayed Taylor Swift as endorsing his campaign, along with fabricated text presenting her as a supporter. Swift had not endorsed him and later backed Kamala Harris. The Guardian reported that the posts used a real person's likeness without consent, illustrating how synthetic images can manufacture apparent political support.
description_long: In August 2024, Donald Trump posted AI-generated images on Truth Social that depicted Taylor Swift and her fans as supporters of his campaign. The posts included fabricated text and used Swift's likeness without her consent; she had not endorsed Trump and later publicly supported Kamala Harris. The Guardian's report also described other deepfakes involving political figures and celebrities, placing the Swift images within a wider set of synthetic campaign-related posts. The distinction between a real endorsement and an image fabricated to suggest one matters during an election: viewers may encounter the image without its context and mistake manufactured support for a genuine statement. Swift's team condemned the use of her likeness, according to the supplied account. The episode shows a candidate sharing synthetic media that falsely represented a public figure's political position. It does not establish that the images changed votes or that Swift's later endorsement was caused by the posts. The linked report supports the event and the attribution; claims about reach, audience belief, or electoral effect would require separate evidence.

title: Trump Calls Journalists 'Scum,' 'Human Garbage,' 'Enemy' at Rallies
description_short: Trump Calls Journalists 'Scum,' 'Human Garbage,' 'Enemy' at Rallies
description_medium: Throughout his first term, Trump used campaign rallies to direct physical hatred at journalists, calling them 'scum,' 'human garbage,' 'the enemy,' and other dehumanizing epithets while crowds cheered and sometimes turned threateningly toward press pens. Numerous journalists reported being surrounded by hostile crowds, receiving death threats, and facing physical intimidation at Trump events. The Committee to Protect Journalists repeatedly issued statements warning that Trump's rhetoric was the most dangerous environment for American journalists since Watergate. Several foreign leaders cited Trump's rhetoric to justify their own crackdowns on domestic press.
